The scene described here is that of the Establishment of the Hour (qiyamah). On that Day the earth will be shaken with extreme violence, and a severe quaking will take place. The earth will throw out whatever lies within its belly, and the burden of human lives that it has carried for a long time, or the minerals within it, it will lift and cast out. It is as though, by casting out this burden, the earth will become light.

This is such a depiction that the listeners feel everything standing upon their feet is unsteady: they sway, they totter, the earth beneath their feet trembles and runs. It is a scene which, upon seeing it, a person cuts off all ties with those affairs that bind him to this earth, and about which he supposes that they are firm and lasting. This is the first of the impressions which the Qur'an seeks to create through such scenes. And upon hearing these unique verses of the Qur'an, this impression passes at once to a person's nerves. This impression becomes still deeper when the Qur'an records the reactions of that "human being" standing in the place of gathering (maydan-i-hashr), who will be seeing these scenes.

"And man will say, 'What is wrong with it?'" This is the question of a person who is stunned by a sudden, terrifying scene, who is witnessing something unseen before, who is confronted with a situation he cannot comprehend, and who is facing a sight on which he can neither remain silent nor exercise patience.

"What is wrong with it?" (مَا لَهَا) — What has happened to it? What is the cause that the earth is in a violent quake, and it is in constant motion, its feet do not remain firm, and it is rolling about from side to side, trying to grasp whatever support comes into its hand; yet everything in its environment is moving, and it is in the grip of a severe earthquake.

Man had already seen earthquakes and volcanic activity, and he has known fear and restlessness during earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. He has seen destruction and ruin. But when he sees the earthquake of the Day of Resurrection, he understands that there is no resemblance between the earthquakes and volcanoes of the world and this present event. This is a different process, a different calamity. He cannot grasp any real cause of this event, and there is no parallel to it. It is an extremely terrifying occurrence, and it is happening for the first time.

On that day (99:4): on the day this earthquake takes place and mankind stands terrified before it. On that day.

Tuhaddithu akhbaraha (99:4): "it will report its news" (i.e., it will relate what has happened upon it). On that day this earth will give its reports, will tell its conditions, and will narrate its entire story.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 99, verse 5:

"Because your Lord has inspired it" (99:5): that is, "Your Lord will have commanded it to do so." It has been commanded to quicken its movement, to shake its surface violently, to throw out what is within it, and it is doing this in obedience to the command of its Lord.

"And it will hearken to its Lord, and it is right that it should": it will obey its Lord's command, and this is its due. Therefore it will relate its circumstances. In short, this situation and this scene vividly demonstrate what Allah's commands and signs will be at that time.

Now the circumstances are such that a person is left astounded. Through the thunderous and forceful description of the Surah, there is an atmosphere of terror and dread; on every side there is a reign of horror and bewilderment. There is agitation and confusion, and in such circumstances a person is left breathless, and he asks what has happened to it.

"What has happened to it?" (99:3): In such circumstances the answer comes in the form of a new scene, namely the scene of gathering and resurrection, reckoning and accounting, and the Balance and recompense.

In a single moment we see people rising from their graves and coming forth.

"On that day people will come forth in scattered groups, so that they may be shown their deeds" (99:6). We see them coming from different directions, in different groups, as though they were scattered locusts.

"As though they were scattered locusts" (101:4). This is a scene that man has never witnessed before: the generations of people, the earlier and the later, rising from here and from there, just as it is stated elsewhere.

"The day the earth splits asunder, and they hasten out of it quickly" (50:44). The scene is that, as far as the eye can see, there are only people: those rising from the graves and hurrying swiftly. No one pays attention to anything else. They look neither ahead nor behind, neither right nor left. Their gazes are raised.

"Hastening, with their heads raised toward the caller" (54:8). Necks stretched high, eyes wide open.

"Every man on that day will have a matter that occupies him completely" (80:37).

This is a scene that cannot be described in any human language. "Terrifying," "frightful," "astonishing," and "stupefying": all such words, and every other word of this kind, are incapable of depicting this scene. Yet we can only push the imagination somewhat further, and in depicting this scene, imagination can roam freely in place of words, within the limits of its own breadth and power.

"On that day people will come forth in scattered groups, so that their deeds may be shown to them" (99:6). And this is even more severe than the scene itself. Alas, their deeds are being presented before them! Will they be able to face their own deeds? Will they be able to withstand that punishment? The truth is that for a person, confronting his own deeds is sometimes the most bitter thing. A person sometimes flees from facing his own deeds, even though no one else knows of them. But when, at the time of repentance and remorse, a person's own deeds stand before him, he is deeply regretful; he flees from his own soul and conscience. How much more so when he must appear in an open court, have his charges read out before everyone, and the presiding judge is the Lord of Majesty and Honour, who is the Compeller and the Proud.

The truth is that merely showing a person his deeds is itself a terrifying punishment: that he should see his whole assembly and face all that he has done. Especially at such a time, when the reckoning is such that every particle is recorded in it, leaving out no particle of evil and no particle of good.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 99, verse 8:

"So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it." (99:7-8)

The older exegetes used to interpret the "dharrah" (atom, mote) as the size of a gnat. They would say that the dharrah is the tiny floating particle which is visible in the rays of the sun. In truth, in that era this was the smallest quantity that those people could imagine. But in today's modern age we know what the dharrah is. It is a definite body, and it is far smaller than the dust particle that floats in the air and is visible in the sunlight, because this tiny quantity floating in the air can only be seen with the naked eye. As for the atom, it can be seen only in a laboratory with a microscope. Scientists in fact see this dharrah with their mind and intellect, and they can see its traces with their eyes. So on the Day of Resurrection, there will be reward and punishment for every good or evil equal to this dharrah, that is, an atom. This small good and evil will also be presented before its doer, and he will see it with his own eyes.

Here every person becomes alert, and does not remain heedless of his good and evil, and does not say that this is a small good deed or a small evil, and it will have no reckoning or accounting. Before this extremely delicate and subtle balance, every person trembles, for even the atom will be weighed and measured there.

In this world there is no balance that can weigh and measure even such an immeasurable atom. However, in the heart of the believer there is a balance of taqwa (God-consciousness), which weighs and measures even the atom, because a believer fears even a sin equal to an atom's weight. Alas, in this world there are hard-hearted people who do not fear crimes like mountains, and there are even cruel-hearted people who are bent on destroying such mountains of goodness before which the tall mountains of this earth are insignificant.

These are extremely hard-hearted, hard like stones. They cling to the earth like stones, and when these hearts come on the Day of Resurrection, they will be crushed to pieces under the weight of their sins. (1)

(1) This paragraph applies to Sayyid Qutb himself, whom Qā'id al-Qalb Nāsir erased from this world, although he was a lofty mountain of goodness.
